title: Multiple Interfaces
story: Your Person type needs to greet ('Hi, I'm Alex') AND display ('Alex, age 25') AND maybe compare by age ('who's older?'). That's three different capabilities. Should you build one giant interface? No! Build three focused interfaces, and let Person satisfy all of them.
why: Real types satisfy multiple interfaces — a Person can be Greetable, Displayable, AND Comparable — and constraining generic functions with multiple interfaces gives you precise, powerful type requirements.
analogy: Multiple interfaces are like certifications on a resume — 'Certified Greeter,' 'Certified Displayable,' 'Certified Comparable.' A candidate (type) can have any combination. A job (function) lists which certifications are required. The hiring manager (compiler) checks that the candidate has all the required certs.
try_it: Add a third interface `Identifiable` with `fn id() -> Int`. Implement it for Person (return age * 1000, or a real ID field). Write a function `fn log_entity[T: Greetable + Displayable + Identifiable](thing: &T)` that prints ID, greeting, and display. What happens if you try to pass a type that only has Greetable — the compiler catches it!
tips: Use `+` to require multiple interfaces: `[T: Greetable + Displayable]` means T must satisfy both
Each interface should be SMALL — if an interface has more than 3 methods, consider splitting it
A type automatically satisfies all interfaces it has methods for — no explicit listing needed
common_mistakes: Creating one mega-interface — 'DoEverything' with 10 methods forces every implementor to write 10 methods
Forgetting the `+` syntax — `[T: Greetable Displayable]` is wrong; use `[T: Greetable + Displayable]`
Adding interface methods that are only used together — if `connect()` is always called before `send()`, they belong in the same interface
